opinions.rationale: A narrower methodological gap remains open, but the statement conflates protocol definition, discretization, and sensitivity analysis. The grace period is part of the sustained treatment strategy: changing it generally changes the adherence rule and causal estimand, so movement across grace periods is not sensitivity of one fixed effect. Grid width can instead be a measurement or numerical-approximation choice, and grid stability is interpretable only when nested grids preserve the treatment strategy, event-ordering convention, and underlying continuous-time estimand. Treatment and visit processes alone cannot guarantee a causally adequate grid because data-generating processes with identical treatment and observation laws can have different within-interval outcome timing. Nevertheless, an outcome-blind selection rule can be prespecified and frozen, after which outcomes can be used to report a multiverse without outcome-driven selection. Coarse intervals do not inevitably reverse treatment-outcome ordering when exact timestamps are retained, and fine intervals do not inevitably create high-dimensional nuisance models or unstable weights; those consequences depend on event-time resolution, model parameterization, and positivity. Misaligned time zero and lost temporal ordering can be critical, but the absence of an automatic selector is a roadmap issue rather than uniformly very-high severity. The literature-wide assertion that no procedure exists is not established under the assigned technical-only lens.
opinions.weakest_true_restatement: Without additional clinical and causal assumptions, treatment and observation processes alone cannot identify a uniquely clinically meaningful grace period or guarantee that a discrete grid preserves relevant treatment-outcome ordering. Analysts can prespecify an outcome-blind grid rule and report post-lock comparisons across plausible same-estimand grids, while alternative grace periods should be presented as different treatment strategies and potentially different estimands.
